ref: DAR — Revelation ch. 15: The Seven Last Plagues
title: The Seven Last Plagues
voicePrompt: In your own words, explain why Smith calls Revelation 15 a 'preparatory scene' for the seven last plagues, and how it shows that the work of mercy has closed while still reassuring God's people of their reward.

questions.stem: According to Smith, what is the role of the fifteenth chapter as a whole?
options: It is but an introduction and solemn preparation for the outpouring of the seven last plagues
It describes the actual pouring out of each of the seven plagues in detail
It records the final judgment of the dead before the great white throne
It recounts the binding of Satan during the millennium
questions.explanation: Smith writes that 'the whole chapter is but an introduction' and 'the most that we here behold is a solemn preparation for the outpouring of these unmixed vials' — the actual pouring out is not yet described here.

questions.stem: Why does Smith say these plagues are manifestations of God's wrath 'without any mixture of mercy'?
options: Because the angels who pour them out are themselves unmerciful beings
Because the temple is opened and the saints have already been judged guilty
Because there is no ministration in the sanctuary during the infliction of the plagues, since no one can enter the temple
Because the plagues fall only upon nations that never heard the gospel
questions.explanation: Smith argues that since 'no man... can enter therein,' the work of mercy is closed — 'there is no ministration in the sanctuary during the infliction of the plagues; hence they are manifestations of the wrath of God without any mixture of mercy.'

questions.stem: How does Smith use verse 5 (the temple being opened) to establish the timing of the plagues?
options: It shows the plagues fall during the height of gospel preaching
It shows the plagues fall after the close of the ministration in the sanctuary, since the temple is opened before they are poured out
It shows the plagues fall before the sanctuary work begins
It shows the plagues fall only after the resurrection of all the dead
questions.explanation: Smith states, 'Verse 5 shows that these plagues fall after the close of the ministration in the sanctuary; for the temple is opened before they are poured out.'

questions.stem: Who gives the seven golden vials to the seven angels, and what significance does Smith attach to this?
options: Christ himself, showing he personally executes vengeance
One of the four beasts (living creatures), who are a class of Christ's assistants in his sanctuary work
The dragon, showing Satan unleashes the plagues
An archangel from the seventh heaven, distinct from the sanctuary
questions.explanation: Smith notes the angels 'receive these vials from one of the four beasts, or living creatures,' which were proved (in chapter 4) to be 'a class of Christ's assistants in his sanctuary work,' making it appropriate they deliver the vials to the ministers of vengeance.

questions.stem: What does Smith say the white linen worn by the seven angels emblematizes?
options: The mourning of heaven over the lost
The mortality of the human victims of the plagues
The purity of God's righteousness and justice in inflicting these judgments
The robe of Christ's own imputed righteousness given to the saints
questions.explanation: Smith writes the angels 'are clothed in linen pure and white, a fit emblem of the purity of God's righteousness and justice in the infliction of these judgments.'

questions.stem: What conclusion does Smith draw from seeing the victors standing on the sea of glass (verses 2-4)?
options: That the saints remain on earth, hidden from the plagues
That the sea of glass is a symbol of the baptismal waters
That the saints are taken to heaven to receive a portion of their reward, since the sea of glass is the one before the throne in chapter 4:6
That the saints are still being tested and have not yet overcome the beast
questions.explanation: Smith identifies the sea of glass as 'the same as that brought to view in chapter 4:6, which was before the throne in heaven,' and concludes 'we have here indubitable proof... that the saints are taken to heaven to receive a portion of their reward.'

questions.stem: According to Smith, what two fields does the song of Moses and the Lamb cover?
options: The field of human history and the field of prophecy
The works of God (his glory, seen in creation/astronomy) and the field of God's providence and grace (his just and true ways)
The fall of Babylon and the gathering of the saints
The judgment of the living and the judgment of the dead
questions.explanation: Smith says the song 'appeals to the works of God which are a manifestation of his glory' (illustrated by astronomy), and 'the song covers another field also — the field of God's providence and grace: "Just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints."'
